intro: Follow a subject containing all twelve chromatic pitch classes through alto, tenor, bass and soprano, with shorter imitations between its full statements. The score is aligned automatically; its provisional timings have not been checked by ear.
question: Can you follow the subject when another voice takes it?

cues.title: Alto: all twelve notes
cues.text: The alto opens alone in B minor, beginning F♯–D–B after a quaver rest. Leaps connect pairs of notes a semitone apart. The complete subject uses all twelve chromatic pitch classes, but its move towards F♯ still gives the line a tonal direction.
cues.evidence: Bars 1–4, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, alto. Its subject contains C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F (written E♯), F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯ and B; B♯ also appears as an enharmonic C. The closing G♯ resolves to F♯ in bar 4. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Tenor answers in F♯ minor
cues.text: The tenor answers in F♯ minor, beginning B–A–F♯. The alto continues with a countersubject — a recurring companion line — whose descending crotchets contrast with the subject’s quavers before breaking into semiquavers. Listen for two independent speeds.
cues.evidence: Bars 4–7, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, tenore starts rest–B–A–F♯–D–B–E–D♯; alto supplies the counter-line, including E–D–C♯–B crotchets in bar 5 and semiquavers in bar 6. This is the tonal answer, not a literal transposition. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Learning in his brother’s household
cues.text: After his father died in 1695, Bach moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist. He learned the organ under his brother’s guidance while attending the local grammar school and singing in its choir.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s chronology, 1695 entry, documents the move, organ lessons and school choir: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Bass subject, two counter-lines
cues.text: The bass states the subject in B minor. Above it, the tenor carries the descending countersubject while the alto adds a quicker companion, mixing dotted notes and semiquavers. Listen for three distinct rhythms, not a melody supported by block chords.
cues.evidence: Bars 9–12, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, basso begins F♯–D–B–G–F♯–B–A♯; tenore descends B–A–G♯–F♯ in bar 10; alto has dotted-quaver and semiquaver figures in bars 9–10. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Soprano completes the four voices
cues.text: The soprano answers in F♯ minor, bringing the subject to the top of the texture. The bass now carries the descending countersubject, while the tenor takes a quicker companion line. The parts change jobs rather than leaving one permanent melody on top.
cues.evidence: Bars 13–16, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, soprano begins B–A–F♯–D–B–E–D♯; basso has E–D–C♯–B crotchets in bar 14; tenore has dotted and semiquaver movement in bar 13. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: An episode in descending sequences
cues.text: Between complete entries, the bass descends through repeating four-note shapes while soprano and tenor imitate a quicker figure. In bar 19 the alto briefly recalls F♯–D–B, the B-minor subject’s opening, then stops: a fragment is not a complete new entry.
cues.evidence: Bars 17–20, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, basso sequences F♯–A–B–D and E–G–A–C♯; soprano and tenore exchange tied-quaver/semiquaver figures. Alto has only rest–F♯–D–B and rests in bar 19. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Alto returns in B minor
cues.text: The alto brings back the complete B-minor subject, again starting F♯–D–B. The soprano supplies the descending countersubject above it. Listen into the middle register: the highest line is not the subject here.
cues.evidence: Bars 21–24, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, alto repeats the opening subject; soprano gives B–A–G♯–F♯ crotchets in bar 22. The cross-voice F♯ tie in bar 23 remains attributed to its originating alto attack in the alignment. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Another episode changes the destination
cues.text: The bass’s rising semiquavers lead into another descending sequence, moving towards E minor. The tenor briefly offers B–G–E in bar 28, an E-minor subject fragment, before withdrawing. Listen for the fuller version that follows.
cues.evidence: Bars 24–29, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, basso begins F♯–G–A–B–C–D and later sequences B–D–E–G, A–C–D–F♯, G–B–C–E and F♯–A–B–D♯. Tenore has rest–B–G–E then rests in bar 28. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Tenor subject in E minor
cues.text: The tenor now gives the full E-minor subject, starting B–G–E. The bass falls silent after its opening E, leaving the inner voice exposed. Above it, the soprano’s descending E–D–C♯–B recalls the countersubject.
cues.evidence: Bars 30–33, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, tenore has B–G–E–C–B–E–D♯ and the chromatic continuation; basso rests after the first crotchet of bar 30; soprano descends in crotchets in bar 31. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Alto and soprano overlap
cues.text: The alto starts a shortened F♯-minor subject in bar 34. One bar later, the soprano enters in B minor before that idea has run its full course. This close imitation, called stretto, packs two recognisable beginnings into less time.
cues.evidence: Bars 34–36, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi. After an initial G♯, alto starts C♯–A–F♯–D–C♯–F♯–E♯; soprano starts rest–F♯–D–B–G–F♯–B–A♯ in bar 35. Both statements shorten the full subject. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: A professional singer at home
cues.text: Bach married the court singer Anna Magdalena Wilcke on 3 December 1721. At the time he was employed at Prince Leopold’s court in Köthen; in 1722 he began seeking another post.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s chronology, 1717 and 1721 entries, documents the Köthen appointment, Anna Magdalena’s profession, the marriage and the subsequent search for work: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Bass returns in B minor
cues.text: The bass’s B-minor entry begins E–D–B, altering the subject’s opening note before recovering its familiar chromatic continuation. The soprano carries the descending countersubject. Follow the low line through its semitone pairs rather than identifying it by its first pitch alone.
cues.evidence: Bars 38–41, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, basso begins E–D–B–G–F♯–B–A♯, then continues E–D♯–C–B–F♯–E♯–D–C♯. Soprano descends B–A–G♯–F♯ in bar 39. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Four overlapping subject entries
cues.text: The subject passes from soprano in B minor, bar 41, to alto in E minor, bar 42; bass in A major, bar 43; and tenor in D major, bar 44. Listen for successive changes of register: each beginning arrives before a full subject’s length has elapsed.
cues.evidence: Bars 41–47, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi. Subject heads begin F♯–D–B in soprano, B–G–E in alto, E–C♯–A in basso and A–F♯–D in tenore at bars 41, 42, 43 and 44 respectively. The first three are shortened; tenor continues through bar 46 into 47. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Bass answer in D major
cues.text: Late in bar 47, the bass begins a D-major answer with D–C♯–A. The soprano carries the descending counter-line above it. The subject keeps its chromatic turns even in this major-key setting; major does not mean that the semitone clashes disappear.
cues.evidence: Bars 47–50, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, basso enters after a minim and quaver rest with D–C♯–A, then F♯–D–G–F♯. Soprano has A–G–F in bar 48 and E–D in bar 49. Timing aligned automatically; the entry is within bar 47, not on its downbeat.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: An episode prepares F♯ minor
cues.text: Running semiquaver figures pass through the voices between subject statements. Listen for short scales curling back on themselves and the alto’s E♯ near the end: the music is moving away from D major towards F♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Bars 50–53, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, soprano runs D–E–F♯–G–A–B–D–C♯; tenor and bass have related scale figures. Alto writes E♯ in bars 52–53 before the tenor’s F♯-minor entry. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Tenor enters in F♯ minor
cues.text: In the second half of bar 53, the tenor starts C♯–A–F♯, the subject in F♯ minor. Its continuation reaches the sharpened leading notes B♯ and F𝄪. Above it, the soprano’s slower G♯–F♯–E–D♯ line recalls the countersubject.
cues.evidence: Bars 53–56, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, tenore starts C♯–A–F♯ after two crotchets and a quaver rest; bar 55 includes B♯ and F𝄪. Soprano descends G♯–F♯–E in bar 54, then D♯–C♯ in bar 55. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Bass subject in E major
cues.text: The bass enters late in bar 57 on B–G♯–E. G♯ makes this an E-major version, distinct from the earlier E-minor entry’s G♮. The soprano counter-line descends above it while the alto keeps faster notes in motion.
cues.evidence: Bars 57–60, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, basso enters after a minim and quaver rest with B–G♯–E, followed by C♯–B–E–D♯. Soprano gives F♯–E–D in bar 58 and C♯–B in bar 59. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Tenor restores B minor
cues.text: Late in bar 60, the tenor starts F♯–D–B, restoring the opening subject in B minor. The soprano and alto continue their own decorated lines above it. Listen beneath the upper activity for the subject’s steady quavers.
cues.evidence: Bars 60–63, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, tenore enters after a minim and quaver rest with F♯–D–B and continues G–F♯–B–A♯ in bar 61. Soprano and alto have independent tied and semiquaver figures. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Music for weekly services
cues.text: Bach’s Leipzig duties from 1723 included cantatas for Sundays and feast days. In 1730 he sent the town council a memorandum describing the resources needed for properly equipped church music. Keyboard counterpoint belonged to a working life that also required regular vocal music.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig’s chronology documents the cantata duties under 1723 and the council memorandum under 1730: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The last extended episode
cues.text: With the bass silent, soprano and alto exchange the episode’s tied-quaver and semiquaver figures. The tenor supplies a descending chain underneath. Listen for the same sequential machinery used earlier, now preparing the last B-minor entries.
cues.evidence: Bars 64–68, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi. Basso rests; soprano and alto sequence the figures prominent in bars 17–20 and 26–29. Tenore has A♯–F♯–B–D–E–G–A–C♯ in bar 65 and descending continuations. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Two low voices overlap
cues.text: The tenor recalls the B-minor subject in bar 69, but gives only its opening portion. The bass follows in E minor at bar 70 with B–G–E. Listen for the subject moving downward through the texture while the soprano supplies the descending countersubject.
cues.evidence: Bars 69–73, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, tenore has F♯–D–B–G–F♯–B–A♯ after an initial B in bar 69; basso begins B–G–E–C–B–E–D♯ in bar 70. Soprano descends E–D–C♯–B in bar 71. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: Alto over a dominant pedal
cues.text: The alto gives one last, shortened B-minor subject, beginning F♯–D–B. Beneath it, the bass holds F♯ across the bar line, a dominant pedal: a sustained foundation that postpones the arrival on B.
cues.evidence: Bars 74–75, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, alto repeats the subject’s first bar and E–D♯ from its continuation before cadential notes replace it. Basso ties F♯ from bar 74 into bar 75. Timing aligned automatically.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

cues.title: The final third is major
cues.text: The last chord settles on B major: D♯ replaces the D♮ of B minor. This raised final third, often called a Picardy third, changes the mode without changing the tonic. The four contrapuntal lines meet in a held chord.
cues.evidence: Bar 76, occurrence 1: Mutopia BWV 869 (1563), notes.lyi, soprano and basso end on B, tenore on F♯, and alto includes D♯ and B. The chord begins at the bar line with fermatas on the outer parts. Timing aligned automatically; the displayed final hold estimates decay, not key release.
cues.how: From the written score, timed by aligning the score to this recording (automatic; not yet checked by ear).

transitions.title: Suspensions carry a descending sequence
transitions.how: After the soprano’s answer, the full subject gives way to a descending sequence. In bars 19–20 the bass repeats F♯–A–B–D, then E–G–A–C♯ a tone lower, before continuing down. Above it, soprano and tenor trade tied quavers and semiquavers. The soprano’s E, tied into bar 20 over D in the bass, resolves down to D: a suspension makes the next step wait. A♯ at the end of the bass sequence leads to B in bar 21, where the alto restores F♯–D–B, the full B-minor subject.
transitions.evidence: The Episodes and alto return boundary is bar 17 at 107.257 s. Mutopia 1563, BWV 869, notes.lyi: soprano/tenore supply the tied-quaver and semiquaver exchanges in 17–20, basso the descending sequence and A♯–B across 20–21, alto the full subject at 21. The E tie crosses 19–20 before its D resolution. The span uses bar-16 and bar-22 times. The analysis shows continuing onset activity around 1:45–2:10 rather than a general pause. The empty relations array does not identify individual entries; these come from the score. Timing remains provisional.

transitions.title: The sequence delivers a lower subject
transitions.how: The bass’s rising semiquavers in bars 24–25 lead back into the episode’s descending machinery. Bar 28 sequences B–D–E–G down to A–C–D–F♯; bar 29 continues G–B–C–E and F♯–A–B–D♯. Soprano and alto carry tied notes across the moving bass: the soprano’s E across bars 26–27 delays its descent to D. The final D♯ in the bass then rises to E in bar 30. After that E, the bass stops; the tenor begins B–G–E, exposing the complete subject in E minor where bar 28 offered only a fragment.
transitions.evidence: The Entries and close imitation boundary is bar 30 at 186.271 s, near the analysis’s 3:06 boundary and E-minor estimates around 3:00–3:10. Mutopia 1563, notes.lyi, basso bars 24–30 writes the scale figures, four-note sequential groups, D♯–E and ensuing rests; soprano ties E across 26–27; tenore has the incomplete B–G–E in 28 and full entry in 30. The span follows bars 24–31 in score.json. The key and voice assignments are score readings, not chroma-derived subject identifications. Automatic timing is provisional.

transitions.title: Running fragments prepare the sharpened leading note
transitions.how: The D-major entry group yields to running fragments rather than a pause. At bar 50 the soprano climbs D–E–F♯–G–A–B before curling back through D–C♯; in 51 the alto answers with E–F♯–G–A–B and a return through E–D♯. Longer tied notes overlap these runs, so one voice keeps sounding while another moves. E♯ in the alto at 52–53 supplies F♯ minor’s leading note. The bass descends A–G♯–F♯ in 53 and withdraws; later in that same bar the tenor begins C♯–A–F♯, turning the episodic movement into a full F♯-minor subject.
transitions.evidence: The Episode and shifted entries boundary is bar 50 at 305.892 s. Mutopia 1563, notes.lyi, soprano 50, alto 51–53, basso 53 and tenore 53 give the stated notes and rests; the tenor entry follows a minim and quaver rest, not the bar’s downbeat. score.json supplies the bar-49-to-54 span. The analysis has a boundary at 5:18, near bar 52 at 317.674 s, and F♯-minor estimates in the approach. These do not independently establish the subject. Bar timing remains provisional.

transitions.title: The tenor becomes the episode’s bass
transitions.how: The bass voice stays silent while the tenor takes over the descending foundation. In bars 65–66 its E–G–A–C♯ pattern is answered lower by D–F♯–G–B, then C♯–E–F♯–A♯. Soprano and alto interlock the earlier episode’s tied quavers and semiquavers above it, retaining motion without a complete subject. The tenor’s final A♯ in bar 68 rises to B in 69, then F♯–D–B recalls the B-minor subject. The actual bass re-enters in bar 70 with B–G–E in E minor: the sequential texture has prepared overlapping low-voice entries, not a full stop.
transitions.evidence: The Final episode and entries boundary is bar 64 at 390.646 s, beside the analysis’s 6:32 novelty boundary. Mutopia 1563, notes.lyi, basso rests through 61–69; tenore supplies the sequential groups in 65–68 and abbreviated B-minor subject at 69; soprano and alto exchange the tied figures; basso enters in E minor at 70. The span uses bar-63 and bar-70 times, reaching the bass re-entry. Continuous onset activity in the analysis supports a connected passage, not a pause. All bar timings remain provisional.

transitions.title: The last suspension resolves into major
transitions.how: The bass climbs D–D♯–E–E♯ in bar 73 to F♯ in 74, tied into 75: a dominant pedal beneath the alto’s last F♯–D–B subject fragment. In bar 75 the soprano holds B over F♯, a fourth above the bass, before resolving to A♯. That suspension delays the dominant’s third. At bar 76 A♯ rises to B, the bass moves F♯–B, and the alto’s final E falls to D♯. The tenor retains F♯. B–D♯–F♯ replaces B minor with B major as the running counterpoint gives way to the fermata chord.
transitions.evidence: The B-major close boundary is bar 76 at 465.118 s; the analysis’s strongest boundary is at 7:46, followed by the final decay. Mutopia 1563, notes.lyi, basso 73–76 gives the chromatic ascent, F♯ tie and final B; soprano 75 gives B–A♯ before the final B; alto ends E–D♯; tenore ties F♯ into 76. The span starts at bar 73 and ends at score.json’s estimated final-chord decay endpoint, 477.360 s, not a measured key release. Score timing is provisional and has not been checked by ear.

scoreSource.title: Das Wohltemperierte Clavier I, Fuga XXIV, BWV 869

facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
